content: The Declaration of Helsinki, as revised in 2008, outlines ethical principles for medical research involving human subjects. It was originally adopted by the World Medical Association (WMA) in 1964 and has undergone multiple amendments to address evolving ethical considerations in medical research. 1. The Declaration of Helsinki was developed by the WMA to establish ethical principles for medical research involving human subjects, including research on identifiable human material and data. It is intended to be read as a whole, with each paragraph considered in the context of the others. 2. While the Declaration is primarily directed at physicians, the WMA encourages all participants in medical research involving human subjects to adopt these principles. 3. Physicians have a duty to promote and safeguard the health of patients, including those involved in medical research. Their knowledge and conscience must be dedicated to fulfilling this duty. 4. Medical progress relies on research involving human subjects. Populations underrepresented in research should be given appropriate opportunities to participate. 5. In medical research involving human subjects, the well-being of the individual research subject must take precedence over all other interests. 6. The primary purpose of medical research involving human subjects is to understand the causes, development, and effects of diseases and to improve preventive, diagnostic, and therapeutic interventions. Even the best current interventions must be continually evaluated for safety, effectiveness, efficiency, accessibility, and quality. 7. Medical research and practice often involve risks and burdens. Ethical standards must be upheld to respect and protect the health and rights of all human subjects, with special protections for vulnerable populations. 8. Physicians must consider ethical, legal, and regulatory norms for research in their own countries and applicable international standards. No national or international requirements should reduce or eliminate protections for research subjects outlined in the Declaration. 9. Physicians involved in medical research must protect the life, health, dignity, integrity, self-determination, privacy, and confidentiality of personal information of research subjects. 10. Medical research involving human subjects must conform to accepted scientific principles, be based on thorough knowledge of the scientific literature, and include adequate laboratory and, where appropriate, animal experimentation. The welfare of animals used in research must be respected. 11. Research protocols must clearly describe the design and performance of each study, including ethical considerations and how the principles of the Declaration are addressed. Protocols should include information on funding, sponsors, institutional affiliations, potential conflicts of interest, subject incentives, and provisions for treating or compensating subjects harmed as a result of participation. 12. Research protocols must be submitted to an independent research ethics committee for review, comment, guidance, and approval before the study begins. This committee must be free from undue influence and have the authority to monitor ongoing studies. Researchers must provide monitoring information, especially regarding serious adverse events, and obtain approval for any protocol changes. 13. Medical research involving human subjects must be conducted only by individuals with appropriate scientific training and qualifications. Research on patients or healthy volunteers requires supervision by a competent and qualified physician or other healthcare professional. Responsibility for the protection of research subjects always rests with the physician or healthcare professional, not the subjects, even if they have given consent. 14. Research involving disadvantaged or vulnerable populations is justified only if it addresses their health needs and priorities and if there is a reasonable likelihood that they will benefit from the research results. 15. Every medical research study involving human subjects must be preceded by a careful assessment of predictable risks and burdens compared to foreseeable benefits for the individuals and communities involved. 16. Clinical trials must be registered in a publicly accessible database before the recruitment of the first subject. 17. Physicians may not participate in research unless they are confident that the risks have been adequately assessed and can be satisfactorily managed. They must stop a study immediately if risks are found to outweigh potential benefits or if conclusive proof of positive results is obtained. 18. Participation in medical research must be voluntary for competent individuals. No competent individual may be enrolled in a study without freely given informed consent. 19. Every precaution must be taken to protect the privacy of research subjects, the confidentiality of their personal information, and to minimize the impact of the study on their physical, mental, and social integrity. 20. Potential research subjects must be adequately informed about the aims, methods, funding sources, potential conflicts of interest, institutional affiliations of the researcher, anticipated benefits, potential risks, and any discomfort the study may entail. They must also be informed of their right to refuse participation or withdraw consent at any time without reprisal. 21. For research using identifiable human material or data, physicians must normally seek consent for collection, analysis, storage, and reuse. In cases where consent is impossible or impractical to obtain, or if it would threaten the validity of the research, the study may proceed only after approval by a research ethics committee. 22. When seeking informed consent, physicians must be cautious if the potential subject is in a dependent relationship with the physician or may consent under duress. In such cases, consent should be sought by an independent, qualified individual. 23. For incompetent potential research subjects, informed consent must be obtained from a legally authorized representative. These individuals should not be included in research that has no likelihood of benefit for them unless it is intended to promote the health of the population they represent, cannot be performed with competent persons, and entails only minimal risk and burden. 24. If an incompetent potential subject can give assent, the physician must seek that assent in addition to the consent of the legally authorized representative. The subject’s dissent must be respected. 25. Research involving subjects who are physically or mentally incapable of giving consent, such as unconscious patients, may proceed only if the condition preventing consent is a necessary characteristic of the research population. In such cases, informed consent must be sought from a legally authorized representative. If no representative is available and the research cannot be delayed, the study may proceed without consent, provided the reasons for involving such subjects are stated in the protocol and the study is approved by a research ethics committee. Consent to remain in the research must be obtained as soon as possible from the subject or a legally authorized representative. 26. Authors, editors, and publishers have ethical obligations regarding the publication of research results. Authors must make their research publicly available and are accountable for the completeness and accuracy of their reports. Negative and inconclusive results, as well as positive results, should be published or otherwise made publicly available. Sources of funding, institutional affiliations, and conflicts of interest must be declared in publications. Research not in accordance with the principles of the Declaration should not be accepted for publication. 27. Physicians may combine medical research with medical care only if the research is justified by its potential preventive, diagnostic, or therapeutic value and if participation in the research is not expected to adversely affect the health of the patients serving as research subjects. 28. The benefits, risks, burdens, and effectiveness of a new intervention must be tested against those of the best current proven intervention, except in cases where no proven intervention exists or where the use of a placebo is necessary for compelling and scientifically sound methodological reasons. Extreme care must be taken to avoid abuse of this option. 29. At the conclusion of a study, patients are entitled to be informed about the study’s outcome and to share in any benefits resulting from it, such as access to beneficial interventions identified in the study or other appropriate care or benefits. 30. Physicians must fully inform patients about which aspects of their care are related to research. A patient’s refusal to participate in a study or decision to withdraw from a study must never interfere with the patient-physician relationship. 31. In the treatment of a patient, where proven interventions do not exist or have been ineffective, a physician may use an unproven intervention if it offers hope of saving life, re-establishing health, or alleviating suffering. This intervention should, where possible, be made the object of research to evaluate its safety and efficacy. New information should be recorded and, where appropriate, made publicly available.
